topic_en: Email: life in a new city
title: News from Lisbon
passage:
Hi Jess,
Sorry it's taken me so long to write! It's been a crazy month. As you know, I moved to Lisbon for my new job in September, and I'm finally starting to feel at home. My flat is small, but it has a tiny balcony where I have breakfast in the sun every morning. The job is going well, although my Portuguese is still terrible, so I mostly speak English at work. I've joined a language exchange group that meets every Thursday in a café near my office. It's a great way to practise and make friends at the same time. Last weekend, a few people from the group took me to a beach just thirty minutes from the city. I couldn't believe how beautiful it was!
Why don't you come and visit in spring? You can stay with me, but I'm afraid you'll have to sleep on the sofa.
Love,
Anna

title: Why slow travel is growing
passage:
More and more people are choosing what is called slow travel. Instead of visiting five cities in a week, slow travellers stay in one place for longer and get to know it properly. They often travel by train or bus rather than by plane, and they see the journey as part of the holiday, not just a way to get somewhere.
Supporters of slow travel say it is less stressful and better for the environment. You spend less time packing and checking in, and more time enjoying local food, markets and conversations with people who live there. Many slow travellers rent a flat instead of staying in a hotel, so they can cook and live like locals.
Of course, slow travel isn't for everyone. It needs more time, and not everyone can take three weeks off work. But even on a short break, you can try some of its ideas: visit fewer places and take your time.

options: Travelling by train is always cheaper than by plane

topic_en: Blog: learning the piano as an adult
topic_ru: Блог: учиться играть на пианино взрослым
title: Never too late
passage:
Last year, just before my fortieth birthday, I finally did something I'd wanted to do since I was a child: I started piano lessons. I was really nervous before the first one. My teacher was about twenty years younger than me, and I was sure I would look silly.
The first few months were hard. My fingers didn't want to do what I asked, and I made the same mistakes again and again. Some evenings I was so tired after work that I didn't practise at all, and then I felt guilty.
But slowly things got better. Now I practise for twenty minutes most days, usually before dinner, and it has become my favourite part of the day. When I play, I forget about emails and deadlines. I'm not going to give concerts, and that's fine. I'm not playing for anyone else, just for me.

questions.q: What is the main message of the blog post?
options: Piano lessons are usually too expensive for busy adults
It's never too late to learn something for yourself
Young teachers are better for adults than older ones
You have to practise every single day to be any good
questions.explain_ru: Автор начал учиться в 40 лет и играет для себя — учиться никогда не поздно.

questions.q: What does playing the piano give the writer now?

title: A morning at Clay Studio
passage:
Last Saturday, my sister and I went to a beginners' pottery workshop at Clay Studio, a small studio in the old part of town. The workshop lasted three hours and cost £45 each, which included all materials and a cup of tea.
The teacher, Rosa, was patient and funny. She showed us how to use the wheel and then let us try on our own. It was much harder than it looks! My first bowl fell apart twice, and by the end I was covered in clay. My sister did much better than me, and she didn't stop talking about it all the way home.
The only disappointing thing was that we couldn't take our bowls home on the day. They need to dry and go in a special oven first, so we have to go back and collect them in two weeks. Still, it was a relaxing and creative morning, and I'd definitely book another class.
